source: NMC guideline 2022; Sarkar OCR; KDT8 ch3, ch5, ch6; Katzung16 ch1, ch66; unsourced items marked

cards.front: What does the NMC prescribe for the OSPE in the MD Pharmacology practical exam?
cards.back: An Objective Structured Practical Examination of 10 to 15 stations, mixing observed stations (an examiner present) and unobserved stations (no observer).
refs: WEB NMC Guidelines for Competency Based PG Training Programme for MD in Pharmacology 01-08-2022 (owner copy: design/NMC-MD-Pharmacology-2022.txt)

cards.front: Classify: example OSPE stations listed by the NMC
cards.text: Drug {{delivery systems}}; calculating {{pharmacokinetic parameters}}; {{pharmaceutical calculations}}; a statistical exercise; {{pharmacoeconomics}}; critical appraisal and {{abstract writing}} of a published paper; evaluating {{drug promotional literature}}; {{ADR reporting and causality assessment}}; assessing {{preclinical toxicity data}}; rational and irrational formulations; choosing a {{P-drug}} and writing a rational prescription; {{analytical instruments}}; spotting ethics dilemmas or mistakes in clinical trial documents.
refs: WEB NMC Guidelines for Competency Based PG Training Programme for MD in Pharmacology 01-08-2022 (owner copy: design/NMC-MD-Pharmacology-2022.txt)

cards.front: Observed versus unobserved OSPE stations: what is assessed at each?
cards.back: Observed: an examiner watches the candidate perform a task (e.g. taking consent, filling an ADR form, preparing a dilution) and scores the process on a fixed checklist. Unobserved: the candidate writes an answer or produces something (a calculation, a critique, an abstract) that is marked later against a key.
refs: WEB NMC Guidelines for Competency Based PG Training Programme for MD in Pharmacology 01-08-2022 (owner copy: design/NMC-MD-Pharmacology-2022.txt)
WEB Indian J Pharmacol Standardization and validation of OSPE in pharmacology 2017 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5754933/
WEB Indian J Pharmacol Introducing OSPE as a method of learning and evaluation for undergraduate pharmacology 2016 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5178055/

cards.front: Why is OSPE preferred to a traditional practical exam?
cards.back: Every candidate does the same tasks, each marked against a pre-set checklist, so marking is more objective. A single written exam does not assess knowledge, skill and attitude together; OSPE stations can.
refs: WEB Indian J Pharmacol Introducing OSPE as a method of learning and evaluation for undergraduate pharmacology 2016 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5178055/
WEB Indian J Pharmacol Standardization and validation of OSPE in pharmacology 2017 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5754933/

cards.front: How should a candidate work through an OSPE station?
cards.back: Read the instruction card fully; note the time allowed; do exactly what is asked (e.g. "identify and give two uses" means two); show steps and units in calculations; for observed stations, say what you are doing (introduce yourself, explain, check understanding); leave the station tidy.
refs: WEB Indian J Pharmacol Standardization and validation of OSPE in pharmacology 2017 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5754933/

cards.front: Short note: Filling a suspected ADR reporting form (PvPI)

points: Initials (not full name), age or date of birth, sex, weight
Description of the event; date of onset and date it stopped
Relevant tests and history; seriousness; outcome
Name (brand and generic), manufacturer, batch number, dose, route, frequency
Dates started and stopped; indication
Dechallenge and rechallenge results
Concomitant drugs, including self-medication
Reporter name, profession, contact details and signature
Handled in confidence; causality assessed at the monitoring centre

cards.front: Under PvPI, what should be reported and who may report?
cards.back: All suspected adverse events with new drugs and "drugs of current interest", all suspected interactions, and reactions to any drug that affect patient management, especially serious ones. Any health care professional (doctor, dentist, nurse, pharmacist) may report; Sarkar notes the programme does not accept reports from lay people.

cards.front: Complete: what makes an adverse reaction "serious"
cards.text: It results in {{death}}, is {{life-threatening}}, causes or prolongs {{hospitalisation}}, causes significant or permanent {{disability}}, causes a {{congenital anomaly}}, or needs {{intervention to prevent permanent damage}}.

cards.front: Trace the path of an ADR report in PvPI.
cards.back: The ADR monitoring centre collects the report, follows it up for completeness and enters it in VigiFlow, sending it to the PvPI National Coordination Centre at IPC Ghaziabad. Data go on to the WHO Uppsala Monitoring Centre database; CDSCO takes regulatory decisions on the NCC's advice.

cards.front: What must an informed consent form for a trial explain to the participant?
cards.back: Purpose of the study; trial treatments and randomisation; procedures; risks; benefits; alternative treatments; compensation or treatment for trial-related injury; the participant's responsibilities; experimental aspects; and any payments.

cards.front: Complete: essential elements of informed consent (Schedule Y)
cards.text: {{Confidentiality}} of the participant; sharing of {{new information}} from the study; {{voluntary}} participation; {{persons to contact}} for study information; rights if {{study-related injury}} occurs; reasons the study may be {{terminated}}; total {{duration}} of the study; total {{number of subjects}}.

cards.front: What appears in the signature part of the prescribed informed consent form?
cards.back: Study title; subject's initials and identifiers (name, date of birth or age); consent statements initialled by the volunteer; signature or thumb impression of the subject or legally acceptable representative; investigator's name and signature; witness's name and signature.

cards.front: Short note: Spotting mistakes in a consent form or trial document (OSPE)

points: Not in the participant's own language, or full of jargon
Consent forms must exist in English and the local language
No statement that participation is voluntary and can be withdrawn without penalty
Risks, alternatives, compensation for injury or contact details left out
Confidentiality not addressed
Coercive wording, excessive payment, or waiving the participant's rights
No witness for an illiterate participant; vulnerable people enrolled without justification
No ethics committee approval

cards.front: Dosage-form or delivery-system identification station: what should your answer cover?
cards.back: Name the dosage form or device, its route, the drug it usually carries and its class, why that form is used (advantage), how to use it correctly, and key precautions or adverse effects.

cards.front: Short note: Drug delivery systems that prolong or target action

points: Sustained-release tablets and spansules (coated particles)
Controlled-release tablets with a semipermeable membrane: part released at once, the rest slowly over hours
Insoluble depot injections (benzathine penicillin, lente insulin) and oily solutions (depot progestins)
Pellets and implants; vasoconstrictor added to a local anaesthetic
Drug-impregnated adhesive patches, e.g. glyceryl trinitrate
Liposomes taken up by reticuloendothelial and some tumour cells (liposomal amphotericin B)
Drug-releasing implants: progestin IUCD; drug-coated stents

cards.front: Which drugs are suited to controlled-release formulations?
cards.back: Drugs with a half-life under about 4 hours benefit; those with a half-life over 12 hours do not need them. Drugs meant for a brief effect (hypnotics, headache remedies) or already long-acting (doxycycline, amlodipine, digoxin) should not be made long-acting.

cards.front: Pharmaceutical calculation: how are percentage and ratio strengths read?
cards.back: % w/v means grams of drug in 100 mL, so a 1% solution is 10 mg/mL. A ratio such as 1 in 1000 means 1 g in 1000 mL, i.e. 1 mg/mL (as for adrenaline 1:1000).

cards.front: How do you make a dilution of a stock solution?
cards.back: Use C1 x V1 = C2 x V2: the stock concentration times the volume taken equals the final concentration times the final volume. Example: to make 10 mL of 0.1 mg/mL from a 1 mg/mL stock, take 1 mL of stock and add diluent to 10 mL. The NMC expects candidates to prepare drug solutions of the right strength and volume.
refs: Ghosh Fundamentals of Experimental Pharmacology PDF p11: stock dilution example

cards.front: How is the final drug concentration in an organ bath calculated?
cards.back: Final bath concentration = (concentration of the solution added x volume added) / volume of the bath. For example, 0.1 mL of a 10 microgram/mL solution in a 10 mL bath gives 0.1 microgram/mL.
refs: Ghosh Fundamentals of Experimental Pharmacology PDF p11: 0.2 mg of 1 mg/mL stock in 10 mL bath = 20 ug/mL
Medhi Practical Manual PDF p87 (printed p71): dilution per organ-bath volume

cards.front: Calculation: a 20 kg child needs a drug whose average adult dose is 500 mg. Dose by body weight?
cards.back: Child dose = 20 / 70 x 500 mg = about 143 mg. KDT prefers weight-based (mg/kg) dosing to age formulae; BSA is used for anticancer drugs.

cards.front: How is an i.v. drip rate calculated?
cards.back: Drops per minute = volume to infuse (mL) x drop factor of the set (drops/mL) / time (minutes). Example: 500 mL over 4 hours with a 20 drops/mL set = 500 x 20 / 240 = about 42 drops per minute.
refs: Dosage Calculations (Pickar) PDF p2: IV flow rate V(mL)/T(min) x C(gtt/mL) = R(gtt/min); visually checked

cards.front: Answering a drug-information query at an OSPE station: what is the approach?
cards.back: Find out who is asking and why, and get patient details; restate the question precisely and classify it (dose, interaction, ADR, pregnancy, availability); search tertiary sources first, then secondary and primary; evaluate the evidence; reply clearly with references; document the query and follow up. A drug information centre works this way.

cards.front: Short note: Evaluating drug promotional literature

points: Every claim backed by evidence with verifiable references
Only approved indications; no "safest" or "best" without data
Graphs not distorted (axes, scales)
Adverse effects, contraindications and precautions stated
Generic name shown clearly, not only the brand
Composition, dose, price, manufacturer present
Evidence from good trials rather than testimonials
Judge against the WHO ethical criteria for medicinal drug promotion
Doctors must tell real information from promotional claims; the NMC lists evaluating promotional literature as a required skill

refs: WEB NMC Guidelines for Competency Based PG Training Programme for MD in Pharmacology 01-08-2022 (owner copy: design/NMC-MD-Pharmacology-2022.txt)

cards.front: What does a package insert contain?
cards.back: Brand and generic names; composition and dosage form; clinical pharmacology; indications; dosage and administration; contraindications; warnings and precautions (including pregnancy, lactation, children, elderly); adverse effects; interactions; overdose and its treatment; storage; presentation; manufacturer. The NMC expects candidates to prepare a package insert.
refs: WEB NMC Guidelines for Competency Based PG Training Programme for MD in Pharmacology 01-08-2022 (owner copy: design/NMC-MD-Pharmacology-2022.txt)

cards.front: What should the label of a dispensed medicine show?
cards.back: Patient name; drug name and strength; dose and directions; quantity; date; and warning labels such as "may cause drowsiness" or "avoid alcohol". A manufacturer's label also carries batch number, manufacturing and expiry dates.

cards.front: Abstract-writing station: how do you write the abstract of a given paper?
cards.back: Use a structured format: background or objective, methods (design, participants, intervention, outcomes), results (main numbers with effect size and confidence interval or P value) and conclusion. Keep to the word limit, make it stand alone, and add no references or claims not in the paper. Sarkar likens a protocol summary of up to 300 words to an abstract.

cards.front: Pharmacoeconomics station: how do you name the analysis from a scenario?
cards.back: Look at how outcomes are measured. Outcomes proven equal and only costs compared: cost-minimisation. Outcome in natural units (cases cured, mmHg, life-years): cost-effectiveness. Outcome in QALYs: cost-utility. Costs and outcomes both in money: cost-benefit.

cards.front: Station: assess given preclinical toxicity data. What do you check?
cards.back: Species (a rodent and a non-rodent) and routes; acute study (dose range, maximum tolerated dose); subacute and chronic studies of a length matching the intended human use, with haematology, biochemistry and histopathology; reproductive and teratogenicity data; mutagenicity (e.g. Ames test); carcinogenicity for long-term drugs; and GLP compliance.

cards.front: Critical appraisal station: which core questions does Sarkar use for a first look at a paper?
cards.back: Is the aim important and interesting? Will the outcome matter clinically? Is the method well designed? Is the primary outcome properly assessed? Is the sample large enough? Is there reason to doubt validity (poor method, small sample, confounding)?

cards.front: Ethics-dilemma station: what faults are typically planted in a trial scenario?
cards.back: No ethics committee approval; consent missing, coerced or not in the local language; vulnerable groups enrolled without justification; placebo used when proven treatment exists; no plan for compensation or care after injury; undeclared conflict of interest; confidentiality not protected.

cards.front: Spectrophotometry: principle.
cards.back: A solution in a cuvette absorbs light of a chosen wavelength, and a photometer measures the light that passes through. By the Beer-Lambert law, absorbance is proportional to the concentration of the substance and the path length, so concentration can be calculated.

cards.front: HPLC: principle and the most common form.
cards.back: An improved column chromatography in which solvent is pumped through a column of very fine particles at high pressure, separating compounds by their affinity for the stationary and mobile phases. Reversed-phase HPLC (non-polar modified silica, polar solvent) is most used. Each compound is identified by its retention time, and the peak gives its amount; HPLC can be coupled to mass spectrometry.

cards.front: Short note: ELISA

points: Antigen-antibody binding gives specificity
An enzyme label (alkaline phosphatase or horseradish peroxidase) turns a substrate into a coloured product, giving sensitivity
Coat wells with antigen
Block unbound sites
Add primary antibody
Add enzyme-linked secondary antibody
Add substrate and read the colour
Direct
Indirect
Sandwich (highly sensitive)
Competitive

cards.front: Thin layer chromatography: principle.
cards.back: Compounds in a mixture move up a coated plate with the solvent by capillary action. Those with more affinity for the stationary phase move slowly, the others faster, so they separate into spots that are then identified by a detection method.

cards.front: Why must OSPE stations and checklists be validated before use?
cards.back: Validity (the station measures what it is meant to) and reliability (consistent results) must be shown. Many pharmacology OSPE stations were not standardised, so each station and checklist should be standardised, piloted and checked. Each station is typically about 5 minutes.
refs: WEB Indian J Pharmacol Standardization and validation of OSPE in pharmacology 2017 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5754933/
